exam: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with new‑onset seizures and a convexity mass on MRI. What is the next best step? — Obtain histology after surgical resection to grade the tumour.
How does the WHO grading of meningioma influence postoperative management? — Grade II/III require adjuvant radiotherapy; Grade I may be observed.

A patient with known HIV presents with a dural‑based lesion lacking a classic dural tail. How do you differentiate meningioma from primary CNS lymphoma? — Perform MRI with contrast and consider stereotactic biopsy; lymphoma often shows homogeneous enhancement without a tail.
What are the key imaging features that separate a meningioma from a dural metastasis? — Meningioma has a broad dural base and a ‘dural tail’; metastasis is often multiple and lacks a tail.
Why is dexamethasone given before meningioma surgery? — To reduce peritumoral edema, decreasing intracranial pressure and improving surgical exposure.

In a low‑resource hospital without MRI, how would you confirm a suspected meningioma? — Use contrast‑enhanced CT to identify a hyperdense extra‑axial mass with a dural attachment; if unavailable, rely on clinical picture and refer for imaging.
What complication is most likely to cause rapid deterioration after a large parasagittal meningioma? — Cerebral herniation due to increasing edema and mass effect.

Explain why routine prophylactic antiepileptic drugs are not always given after meningioma resection. — Evidence shows they do not reduce long‑term seizure risk and increase side‑effects; they are used only if seizures occurred pre‑operatively.
ai.title: Meningioma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Meningioma is a usually benign extra‑axial tumor arising from arachnoid cap cells. It presents with focal neurological signs depending on location and may cause life‑threatening brain herniation if large.

b: Often iso‑ to hypointense on T1, iso‑ to hyperintense on T2
sections.p: A meningioma is a dural‑based neoplasm that originates from arachnoid villi. Diagnosis rests on imaging showing a well‑circumscribed extra‑axial mass with a dural tail, and histology confirming meningothelial, fibroblastic, or transitional cells.

b: Grade I: low mitotic index, no necrosis
Grade II: ≥4 mitoses/10 HPF or brain invasion
Grade III: ≥20 mitoses/10 HPF, frank malignancy
sections.p: The WHO grading system (I‑III) predicts behaviour: Grade I (benign, 80‑90 %), Grade II (atypical, higher recurrence), Grade III (anaplastic, malignant). Size, edema, and location influence surgical risk.

Most meningiomas are sporadic. Recognised risk factors are prior cranial irradiation and, rarely, neurofibromatosis type 2. In low‑resource settings, HIV‑related immunosuppression may increase incidence.

b: Seizure in a previously healthy adult
sections.p: Symptoms reflect mass effect and location: seizures (convexity lesions), focal weakness, visual field loss (parasagittal), cranial‑nerve palsies (skull‑base), or headache from raised intracranial pressure.

t.b: Is there a hyperdense extra‑axial mass? → Confirms presence, useful where MRI unavailable.
What is the exact size, dural attachment, and edema? → Gold standard for planning surgery.
What is the WHO grade? → Guides need for adjuvant radiotherapy.
Is immunosuppression present? → May affect prognosis and postoperative care.

sections.p: Rapid neurological decline, new focal deficits, or signs of herniation demand urgent intervention.

b: Craniotomy with Simpson grade I–IV resection
Fractionated external beam radiotherapy for residual or atypical lesions
sections.p: Surgery is first‑line for symptomatic or large lesions. For Grade II/III or unresectable tumors, postoperative radiotherapy is indicated. Steroids reduce peritumoral edema pre‑operatively.
Post‑operative MRI at 3 months, then annually for Grade I; more frequent imaging for higher grades. No proven primary prevention; avoid unnecessary cranial irradiation.

b: Dural metastasis: often multiple, history of cancer
Hemangioblastoma: cystic component, strong flow voids
Vestibular schwannoma: presents with hearing loss, not seizures
sections.p: Differential diagnoses include dural metastasis, hemangioblastoma, and vestibular schwannoma (when at the cerebellopontine angle).

b: CT without contrast may underestimate size
HIV‑related lesions may lack classic dural tail
sections.p: Small meningiomas may be missed on non‑contrast CT; edema can be mistaken for primary brain tumour. In HIV patients, atypical imaging may mimic lymphoma.
